questions.prompt: The review multiplies matrices by the row-column rule. For blocks that fit, the product \(\begin{bmatrix} A & B \\ C & D \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} E & F \\ G & H \end{bmatrix}\) equals
questions.explanation: Each block row meets each block column, and the products add, just as scalar entries do. The upper-left block is \(AE+BG\), not \(AE\) alone. Adding the blocks is the sum of the two matrices, which is a different operation. Entrywise products ignore the inner dimension that matrix multiplication uses.

questions.explanation: The upper-left entry is \(1\cdot 4 + 2\cdot 1 = 6\). The product \(1\cdot 4 = 4\) drops the second term. The upper-right entry is \(1\cdot 0+2\cdot 5 = 10\). The lower-left entry is \(0\cdot 4+3\cdot 1 = 3\).

questions.prompt: When the upper-left block \(A\) is invertible, the Schur complement of \(A\) in \(\begin{bmatrix} A & B \\ C & D \end{bmatrix}\) is
questions.explanation: The complement of the invertible upper-left block is the lower-right block after the elimination step \(D-CA^{-1}B\). The complement of \(D\) would subtract from \(A\), and it needs \(D\) to be invertible, which is not the hypothesis. Swapping \(A\) with \(B\) uses a block the definition does not invert. Multiplying \(A^{-1}\) by \(D\) is not the elimination correction.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>scalar blocks</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">5   2</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">10   9</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A 2 by 2 matrix with entries 5, 2, 10, and 9.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order that computes the Schur complement of the upper-left block A.
questions.explanation: The inverse has to exist before it can be multiplied by B. That product is what C then multiplies on the left. The subtraction removes the finished product from D, so it is last. Multiplying C by A before inverting A is a different association and is not one of these steps. Subtracting before the product exists leaves nothing to subtract.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>scalar blocks</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">5   2</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">10   9</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A 2 by 2 matrix with entries 5, 2, 10, and 9.
steps: Multiply that inverse on the right by the upper-right block B.
Multiply the lower-left block C on the left of that product.
Subtract the resulting product from the lower-right block D.

questions.prompt: The blocks are the scalars \(A=5\), \(B=2\), \(C=10\), and \(D=9\). What is the Schur complement of \(A\)?
questions.explanation: The complement is \(9-10\cdot(1/5)\cdot 2 = 9-4 = 5\). Stopping at \(10/5 = 2\) forgets to multiply by \(B\) and to subtract from \(D\). The difference \(9-2 = 7\) subtracts \(B\) rather than \(CA^{-1}B\). The product \(10\cdot 2 = 20\) never inverts \(A\).
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>scalar blocks</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">5   2</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">10   9</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A 2 by 2 matrix with entries 5, 2, 10, and 9.

questions.prompt: For those same scalar blocks, the lower-right entry of the inverse is the reciprocal of the Schur complement. What is that entry?
questions.explanation: The complement is 5, and the lower-right entry of the inverse is \(1/5 = 0.2\). The complement 5 itself sits in the factored block diagonal, not in the inverse. The reciprocal of the block \(A\) is also \(1/5\) in this example, because the complement happens to equal \(A\). The identity being used is the reciprocal of the complement. The product \(5\cdot 9 = 45\) is not an entry of the inverse.

questions.prompt: Let \(a\), \(b\), \(c\), and \(d\) be the four scalar blocks, with \(a \ne 0\). Write the Schur complement of \(a\) as an expression in a, b, c, and d.
questions.explanation:
For scalars the complement is \(d-c a^{-1} b\), which is \(d-(c b)/a\).
• \(d-c-b+a\) treats the blocks as a sum.
• \(d-c\cdot b\) forgets to invert \(a\).
• \((d-c)/a\) divides the wrong difference and drops \(b\).

questions.prompt: The upper-left block \(A\) is invertible, and \(S = D-CA^{-1}B\) is invertible. Which statements are true?
questions.explanation: Invertibility of \(A\) and of the Schur complement is the block test for invertibility, and the determinant factors as \(\det(A)\det(S)\). The inverse formula puts \(S^{-1}\) in the lower-right corner. Entrywise products are not matrix products.

questions.figure_alt: A 2 by 2 matrix with entries 5, 2, 10, and 9.
options: The whole block matrix is invertible.
The blocks multiply by the entrywise product.
The lower-right block of the inverse is \(S^{-1}\).

questions.prompt: A symmetric block matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} A & B \\ B^T & D \end{bmatrix}\) with \(A\) positive definite is itself positive definite exactly when
questions.explanation: Completing the square in the quadratic form leaves the form of \(A\) plus the form of the Schur complement. Both must be positive definite. A positive trace of \(D\) does not control the complement. \(D\) need not be diagonal. \(B\) may be nonzero; the complement subtracts the correction \(B^T A^{-1} B\) instead of requiring \(B = 0\).
options: the Schur complement \(D-B^T A^{-1} B\) is positive definite

questions.prompt: One step below is false. Select that step, and the reason it fails. The blocks are the scalars \(A=5\), \(B=2\), \(C=10\), and \(D=9\).
questions.explanation: The entry 5 is invertible, and the complement really is \(9-10\cdot(1/5)\cdot 2\). That product is 4, so the complement is \(9-4 = 5\), not \(9-1\). A nonzero complement is the right invertibility test for this 2 by 2 matrix once the upper-left entry is nonzero. The arithmetic step is the false one.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>scalar blocks</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">5   2</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">10   9</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A 2 by 2 matrix with entries 5, 2, 10, and 9.
steps: The Schur complement of that entry is 9 - 10*(1/5)*2.
That value equals 9 - 1, so the complement is 8.
The 2 by 2 matrix is invertible because this complement is nonzero.
reasons: The product 10*(1/5)*2 equals 4, so the complement is 5, not 8.
The Schur complement adds the product to D, so the minus sign is the mistake.
A 2 by 2 matrix is invertible exactly when the upper-left entry is nonzero, and the complement is irrelevant.

questions.prompt: Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}\), \(C = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), and \(D = \begin{bmatrix} 11 \end{bmatrix}\). A later semidefinite constraint needs the Schur complement of \(A\). What is that complement?
questions.explanation: \(A^{-1} = \mathrm{diag}(1,1/2)\), so \(A^{-1}B = (2,1)\). Then \(C A^{-1} B = 1\cdot 2+2\cdot 1 = 4\), and \(S = 11-4 = 7\). The value 11 is \(D\) before the correction. The product \(2\cdot 2 = 4\) happens to equal the correction, but only after \(A^{-1}\) is applied; subtracting \(B\)'s first entry alone gives \(11-2 = 9\). The determinant of \(A\) is 2, which is not the complement.

questions.prompt: A semidefinite constraint can say that a symmetric block matrix is positive semidefinite. When the upper-left block is positive definite, that constraint is the same as a constraint on
questions.explanation: Positive definiteness of the upper-left block together with positive semidefiniteness of its Schur complement is the block test. The trace of one block does not see the coupling. The product of the four blocks is not a congruence. The sum of the off-diagonal blocks cancels in a symmetric matrix only when they are opposites, and that sum is not the complement.
options: the trace of the upper-left block alone
the Schur complement of the upper-left block
the product of all four blocks
the sum of the off-diagonal blocks
